name: Work with existing CRDs (discover & validate)
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration and Security. Drill EVERY CRD corner harder than the exam: author a typed CRD, create and inspect CRs, discover an installed CRD, list via plural/short name, enforce schema validation (required + enum), cluster-scoped CRDs, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix on a CRD that won't serve. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Discover a CRD already on the cluster
questions.teach:
On real clusters operators install their own CRDs you must discover blind: `kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com` lists the kinds, and `kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com -o yaml` reveals the schema. Then create CRs against the discovered group/version.

**Gotcha:** a CR's `apiVersion` is the group plus the version where `served: true` (`demo.example.com/v1`) — read it off the CRD, don't guess.
questions.prompt:
Setup already installed a CRD for kind `Gizmo` in group `demo.example.com` (plural `gizmos`, namespaced, `spec.power` integer). Discover it, then create a `Gizmo` named `turbo` in `crd-learn` with `spec.power: 9`.

Target: `kubectl -n crd-learn get gizmo turbo` exists with `.spec.power == 9`.
questions.hint: Find it: `kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com`. Inspect: `kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com -o yaml`. Then apply a `demo.example.com/v1` `Gizmo` with `spec.power: 9`.
questions.solution:
kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f -
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1
kind: Gizmo
metadata:
  name: turbo
spec:
  power: 9
YAML
kubectl -n crd-learn get gizmo turbo -o jsonpath='{.spec.power}'

verification.description: Gizmo 'turbo' (seeded CRD) in crd-learn with power=9

questions.eli5:
In the real world you rarely write the instruction card yourself. Usually some tool (an "operator") already handed one to the clerk before you arrived, and now you have to figure out what new kinds exist and how to use them — like walking into a kitchen and reading the menu the chef already wrote, instead of inventing dishes.

So this is detective work:

- **"What new dishes are on the menu?"** → `kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com` lists the kinds in that family.
- **"What exactly does this dish need?"** → `kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com -o yaml` shows you the full card: its group, its served version, and the shape of its `spec`.

Once you've *read* it, you order like normal: a `Gizmo` named `turbo` with `spec.power: 9`, using the group and version you found on the card.

**Watch out:**

- **Don't guess the `apiVersion`.** Read it off the CRD: it's the group plus the version that has `served: true` (here `demo.example.com/v1`). Guessing `v1beta1` when it's `v1` fails.
- The **kind** and **field names** must match the card exactly — `Gizmo` with `spec.power`, not `power-level`.
- `Gizmo` is **namespaced**, so create and fetch it with `-n crd-learn`.
- `api-resources` tells you the plural, short names, and whether it's namespaced — use it before anything else so you're not flying blind.
- If nothing shows up, double-check the **group name** you passed to `--api-group`; a typo there returns an empty list, not an error.
questions.deepDive:
## Discovering an installed CRD — full rundown

### Mental model
On real clusters, operators and Helm charts install their own CRDs before you ever touch them. Your job is to **discover** the kind blind: find its group/version/plural, read its schema, then create conformant CRs. The apiserver's **discovery** endpoints (`api-resources`) and the CRD object itself (`get crd -o yaml`) are your two sources of truth — never guess.

### Step 1 — discover the kinds in a group
```bash
kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com
# NAME     SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION              NAMESPACED   KIND
# gizmos                demo.example.com/v1     true         Gizmo
```
This one command gives you the **plural**, **shortNames**, **APIVERSION** (group/version), **NAMESPACED** flag, and **KIND** — everything needed to write a CR.

Other discovery commands:
```bash
kubectl get crd                                   # all CRDs on the cluster
kubectl get crd | grep demo.example.com           # filter by group
kubectl explain gizmo.spec                         # schema-driven field docs
```

### Step 2 — read the schema
```bash
kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com -o yaml
```
Look for:
| Where | Tells you |
|---|---|
| `spec.group` | the API group |
| `spec.versions[].name` + `served:true` | which version to put in the CR's `apiVersion` |
| `spec.scope` | Namespaced vs Cluster |
| `spec.names.kind` | the CR's `kind` |
| `spec.versions[].schema.openAPIV3Schema` | required/typed fields |

Narrow the schema fast:
```bash
kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[?(@.served)].name}'; echo       # served version
kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[0].schema.openAPIV3Schema.properties.spec.properties}'; echo
```

### Step 3 — create a conformant CR
```yaml
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1     # group + SERVED version, read off the CRD
kind: Gizmo
metadata:
  name: turbo
  namespace: crd-learn              # it's Namespaced
spec:
  power: 9                          # integer per schema
```
```bash
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f turbo.yaml
kubectl -n crd-learn get gizmo turbo -o jsonpath='{.spec.power}'
```

### Determining the right apiVersion
`apiVersion` = `spec.group` + `/` + the version whose `served: true`. A CRD may serve several versions; pick a served one (usually the storage version). Never assume `v1` — some ship `v1alpha1`/`v1beta1`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Guessing the version** instead of reading it → `no matches for kind`. Always confirm via `api-resources` or the CRD.
- **`--api-group` typo** returns an empty list silently (not an error) — looks like "nothing installed."
- **Wrong scope assumption**: check `spec.scope` before deciding whether to pass `-n`.
- **Field/type drift**: match `spec` field names and types to the schema exactly; structural schemas prune unknown fields.
- `kubectl explain <kind>` works for CRDs too — fast way to see expected fields without reading raw YAML.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl api-resources --api-group=demo.example.com     # discover kind/version/scope
kubectl get crd gizmos.demo.example.com -o yaml        # full schema
kubectl explain gizmo.spec                              # field docs
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f turbo.yaml               # create conformant CR
```

questions.title: Schema validation: required field + enum
questions.teach:
An `openAPIV3Schema` enforces data: `required: [model]` rejects CRs missing that field, and `enum: [eco, turbo]` rejects any other value. The API server validates on apply, so a bad CR fails fast with a clear error.

**Gotcha:** the seeded `Robot` CRD requires `spec.model` and restricts `spec.mode` to `eco`/`turbo` — a CR missing `model` or using `mode: fast` is rejected; your CR must satisfy both.
questions.prompt:
Setup installed a namespaced CRD `robots.demo.example.com` (kind `Robot`) whose schema **requires** `spec.model` (string) and restricts `spec.mode` to the enum `eco` or `turbo`. Create a valid `Robot` named `r2d2` in `crd-learn` with `spec.model: astromech` and `spec.mode: turbo`.

Target: `kubectl -n crd-learn get robot r2d2` exists with `.spec.model == astromech` and `.spec.mode == turbo`.
questions.hint: Inspect the schema with `kubectl get crd robots.demo.example.com -o yaml`. Apply a `demo.example.com/v1` `Robot` with `spec.model: astromech` and `spec.mode: turbo` (both required/valid-enum).
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f -
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1
kind: Robot
metadata:
  name: r2d2
spec:
  model: astromech
  mode: turbo
YAML
kubectl -n crd-learn get robot r2d2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.model}/{.spec.mode}'

verification.description: Robot 'r2d2' in crd-learn with model=astromech, mode=turbo (passed required+enum validation)

questions.eli5:
Some instruction cards are picky about what you're allowed to write on the order form. Think of ordering a coffee where the barista's form has rules printed on it:

- **"Name is required"** — you *must* fill in a field, or they hand the form back.
- **"Size: small or large only"** — you may only pick from a fixed list; write "ginormous" and it's rejected on the spot.

A CRD schema does exactly this. **`required: [model]`** means a `Robot` with no `spec.model` is refused. **`enum: [eco, turbo]`** means `spec.mode` must be `eco` or `turbo` — `fast` is rejected. The clerk (the API server) checks the moment you hand in the form, so a bad Robot fails immediately with a clear message, nothing gets stored.

To make a *valid* Robot you satisfy **both** rules: give it `spec.model: astromech` (required field present) and `spec.mode: turbo` (a value from the allowed list).

**Watch out:**

- **Required means required** — leave out `spec.model` and the whole apply fails, even if everything else is perfect.
- **Enum is a closed list** — only the exact spelled values work. `Turbo` (capital T) or `fast` both fail; it's case-sensitive and exact.
- Read the real rules first with `kubectl get crd robots.demo.example.com -o yaml` (or `kubectl explain robot.spec`) — don't assume which fields are required or what the allowed values are.
- The error message names the offending field — read it; it tells you exactly what to fix.
- `Robot` is namespaced, so keep `-n crd-learn` on both create and get.
questions.deepDive:
## CRD schema validation: required fields + enum — full rundown

### Mental model
The CRD's `openAPIV3Schema` isn't just documentation — the apiserver **enforces** it on every write. `required` makes fields mandatory; `enum` restricts a field to a fixed set of values; `type` constrains the data type. A CR that violates any constraint is **rejected at apply time** (nothing is stored), with an error naming the field.

### What the schema looks like (on the CRD)
```yaml
schema:
  openAPIV3Schema:
    type: object
    properties:
      spec:
        type: object
        required: [model]              # spec.model MUST be present
        properties:
          model:
            type: string
          mode:
            type: string
            enum: [eco, turbo]         # only these two values allowed
```

### A CR that passes both constraints
```yaml
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1
kind: Robot
metadata:
  name: r2d2
  namespace: crd-learn
spec:
  model: astromech                     # satisfies required
  mode: turbo                          # a valid enum value
```
```bash
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f r2d2.yaml
kubectl -n crd-learn get robot r2d2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.model}/{.spec.mode}'
```

### Common OpenAPI v3 validation keywords
| Keyword | Effect | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | data type | `type: integer` |
| `required` | fields that must be set | `required: [model]` |
| `enum` | closed set of allowed values | `enum: [eco, turbo]` |
| `minimum` / `maximum` | numeric bounds | `minimum: 1` |
| `minLength` / `maxLength` | string length | `maxLength: 32` |
| `pattern` | regex for strings | `pattern: '^[a-z]+$'` |
| `default` | value applied if omitted | `default: eco` |

### What rejection looks like
```bash
# missing required field:
# The Robot "r2d2" is invalid: spec.model: Required value
# bad enum value (mode: fast):
# spec.mode: Unsupported value: "fast": supported values: "eco", "turbo"
```
The message always names the exact field and constraint.

### Inspecting the constraints before you write
```bash
kubectl get crd robots.demo.example.com -o yaml          # full schema
kubectl explain robot.spec                                # field docs
kubectl explain robot.spec.mode                           # shows enum/type
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Omitting a `required` field** fails the whole apply — even one missing required field blocks everything.
- **Enum is exact + case-sensitive**: `turbo` ✅, `Turbo` ❌, `fast` ❌.
- **Pruning vs validation**: with a structural schema, *unknown* fields are silently pruned, but *invalid values* on known fields are *rejected* — different behaviors.
- **`default`** can fill a field you omitted; check for defaults before assuming a field is required.
- **Read the schema, don't guess** which fields are required or what values enums allow.
- Keep `-n` on namespaced kinds for both create and verify.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl explain robot.spec                 # see required + enum quickly
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f r2d2.yaml    # model=astromech, mode=turbo
kubectl -n crd-learn get robot r2d2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.model}/{.spec.mode}'
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a CRD that won't serve
questions.teach:
A CRD can be installed and Established yet still refuse to create CRs when its only version has `served: false` — the REST endpoint isn't exposed, so `kubectl apply` fails with `the server could not find the requested resource`. Flip that version's `served` to `true`.

**Gotcha:** `served` and `storage` are independent per-version flags; a version can be the storage version but still be unserved. Patch the CRD, don't recreate it.
questions.prompt:
Setup installed a namespaced CRD `sprockets.demo.example.com` (kind `Sprocket`, `spec.teeth` integer), but creating a `Sprocket` fails. Diagnose why and fix the CRD so its `v1` is served, then create a `Sprocket` named `sp1` in `crd-learn` with `spec.teeth: 12`. Do not delete and recreate the CRD — patch it.

Target: CRD `sprockets.demo.example.com` version `v1` has `served: true`, and `kubectl -n crd-learn get sprocket sp1` exists with `.spec.teeth == 12`.
questions.hint: `kubectl get crd sprockets.demo.example.com -o yaml` → `versions[0].served: false`. Patch it: `kubectl patch crd sprockets.demo.example.com --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/versions/0/served","value":true}]'`. Then apply the `demo.example.com/v1` `Sprocket` with `spec.teeth: 12`.
questions.solution:
# The only version has served:false, so no REST endpoint exists for Sprocket.
kubectl patch crd sprockets.demo.example.com --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/versions/0/served","value":true}]'
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/sprockets.demo.example.com --timeout=30s
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f -
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1
kind: Sprocket
metadata:
  name: sp1
spec:
  teeth: 12
YAML
kubectl -n crd-learn get sprocket sp1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.teeth}'

verification.description: sprockets CRD v1 served=true; Sprocket sp1 in crd-learn with teeth=12

questions.eli5:
Here's a sneaky one. The clerk has the instruction card, the card is accepted and filed (`Established: True`), everything *looks* fine — yet when you try to create a Sprocket, you get "the server could not find the requested resource." Huh?

Think of a shop that's registered with the city and has its name on the directory, but the **front door is locked** and the "Open" sign is off. The business legally exists, but no customer can actually walk in and buy anything.

On a CRD, that "Open sign" is the version's **`served` flag**. If the only version has `served: false`, the API server never opens a REST door for that kind — so `kubectl apply` can't find anywhere to send your Sprocket. The fix is simply to flip the sign on: set that version's `served` to `true`.

And you **patch** the existing card rather than tearing it up and writing a new one — like flipping the open sign without demolishing the shop.

**Watch out:**

- **`served` and `storage` are separate switches.** A version can be the filing cabinet (`storage: true`) yet still have its door locked (`served: false`). Don't confuse the two.
- The symptom — **"server could not find the requested resource"** even though `kubectl get crd` shows it — is the classic sign of `served: false`. Read the CRD YAML to confirm.
- **Patch, don't recreate.** Deleting the CRD would delete all its custom resources. Use `kubectl patch`.
- After patching, give it a moment / `kubectl wait --for=condition=Established` before creating the CR.
- At least **one** version must be served for the kind to be usable at all.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: a CRD that won't serve — full rundown

### Mental model
A CRD can be **present and Established** yet still refuse to create CRs. `Established` only means the *name* is registered and recognized by discovery — it does **not** mean any version is reachable. Whether a REST endpoint actually exists for a version is controlled by that version's **`served`** flag. `served: false` → no endpoint → `kubectl apply` fails with `the server could not find the requested resource`, even though `kubectl get crd` shows the CRD.

### Diagnosis workflow
```bash
# 1. The CRD exists and is Established...
kubectl get crd sprockets.demo.example.com

# 2. ...but creating a CR fails:
#    error: ... the server could not find the requested resource

# 3. Inspect the versions — find served:false
kubectl get crd sprockets.demo.example.com -o yaml | grep -A4 'versions:'
kubectl get crd sprockets.demo.example.com \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.versions[*]}{.name}{" served="}{.served}{" storage="}{.storage}{"\n"}{end}'
# v1 served=false storage=true   <- the problem
```

### `served` vs `storage` — two independent flags
| Flag | Controls | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `served` | Is this version exposed over REST / usable by clients? | at least **one** version must be `true` to use the kind |
| `storage` | Is this the version persisted in etcd? | **exactly one** version must be `true` |

A version can be `storage: true, served: false` (stored but not reachable) — that is exactly the fault here.

### The fix — patch, don't recreate
```bash
kubectl patch crd sprockets.demo.example.com --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/versions/0/served","value":true}]'

kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/sprockets.demo.example.com --timeout=30s
```
Alternative — open and flip `served: true` by hand:
```bash
kubectl edit crd sprockets.demo.example.com
```

### Create the CR after fixing
```yaml
apiVersion: demo.example.com/v1
kind: Sprocket
metadata:
  name: sp1
  namespace: crd-learn
spec:
  teeth: 12
```
```bash
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f sp1.yaml
kubectl -n crd-learn get sprocket sp1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.teeth}'    # 12
```

### Why not delete and recreate?
Deleting a CRD **cascade-deletes every CR of that kind**. In the exam (and in production) that's data loss. Always `patch`/`edit` to change CRD fields; recreate only when scope or an immutable field must change and you accept the loss.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Established ≠ usable.** The symptom is `could not find the requested resource` with the CRD clearly present.
- **`served` vs `storage` confusion** — the broken version is often the storage version, which misleads you into thinking it's fine.
- **JSON patch path** uses the version **index**: `/spec/versions/0/served`. Get the index right if multiple versions exist.
- **Never delete the CRD** to "reset" it — you lose all CRs.
- After patching, **wait for Established** again before applying CRs to avoid a race.
- If multiple versions exist, ensure the one you serve is also a sensible storage/conversion setup.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get crd sprockets.demo.example.com \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.versions[*]}{.name}{" served="}{.served}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl patch crd sprockets.demo.example.com --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/versions/0/served","value":true}]'
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/sprockets.demo.example.com --timeout=30s
kubectl -n crd-learn apply -f sp1.yaml
```
